text:
Since the beginning of the generative AI boom, there has been a fight over how large AI models are trained. In one camp sit tech companies such as OpenAI that have claimed it is “impossible” to train AI without hoovering the internet of copyrighted data. And in the other camp are artists who argue that AI companies have taken their intellectual property without consent and compensation. 

Adobe is pretty unusual in that it sides with the latter group, with an  approach that stands out as an example of how generative AI products can be built without scraping copyrighted data from the internet. Adobe released its image-generating model Firefly, which is integrated into its popular photo editing tool Photoshop, one year ago.

In an exclusive interview with MIT Technology Review, Adobe’s AI leaders are adamant this is the only way forward. At stake is not just the livelihood of creators, they say, but our whole information ecosystem. What they have learned shows that building responsible tech doesn’t have to come at the cost of doing business. 

“We worry that the industry, Silicon Valley in particular, does not pause to ask the ‘how’ or the ‘why.’ Just because you can build something doesn’t mean you should build it without consideration of the impact that you’re creating,” says David Wadhwani, president of Adobe’s digital media business. 

Those questions guided the creation of Firefly. When the generative image boom kicked off in 2022, there was a major backlash against AI from creative communities. Many people were using generative AI models as derivative content machines to create images in the style of another artist, sparking a legal fight over copyright and fair use. The latest generative AI technology has also made it much easier to create deepfakes and misinformation. 

It soon became clear that to offer creators proper credit and businesses legal certainty, the company could not build its models by scraping the web of data, Wadwani says.  

Adobe wants to reap the benefits of generative AI while still “recognizing that these are built on the back of human labor. And we have to figure out how to fairly compensate people for that labor now and in the future,” says Ely Greenfield, Adobe’s chief technology officer for digital media.  

To scrape or not to scrape

The scraping of online data, commonplace in AI, has recently become highly controversial. AI companies such as OpenAI, https://t.co/G133p3BVPF, Meta, and Google are facing numerous lawsuits over AI training data. Tech companies argue that publicly available data is fair game. Writers and artists disagree and are pushing for a license-based model, where creators would get compensated for having their work included in training datasets. 

Adobe trained Firefly on content that had an explicit license allowing AI training, which means the bulk of the training data comes from Adobe’s library of stock photos, says Greenfield. The company offers creators extra compensation when material is  used to train AI models, he adds.  

This is in contrast to the status quo in AI today, where tech companies scrape the web indiscriminately and have a limited understanding of what of what the training data includes. Because of these practices, the AI datasets inevitably include copyrighted content and personal data, and research has uncovered toxic content, such as child sexual abuse material. 

Scraping the internet gives tech companies a cheap way to get lots of AI training data, and traditionally, having more data has allowed developers to build more powerful models. Limiting Firefly to licensed data for training was a risky bet, says Greenfield. 

“To be honest, when we started with Firefly with our image model, we didn’t know whether or not we would be able to satisfy customer needs without scraping the web,” says Greenfield. 

“And we found we could, which was great.” 

Human content moderators also review the training data to weed out objectionable or harmful content, known intellectual property, and images of known people, and the company has licenses for everything its products train on. 

Adobe’s strategy has been to integrate generative AI tools into its existing products, says Greenfield. In Photoshop, for example, Firefly users can fill in areas of an image using text commands. This allows them much more control over the creative process, and it aids their creativity. 

Still, more work needs to be done. The company wants to make Firefly even faster. Currently it takes around 10 seconds for the company’s content moderation algorithms to check the outputs of the model, for example, Greenfield says. Adobe is also trying to figure out how some business customers could generate copyrighted content, such as Marvel characters or Mickey Mouse. Adobe has teamed up with companies such as IBM, Mattel, NVIDIA and NASCAR, which allows these companies to use the tool with their intellectual property. It is also working on audio, lip synching tools and  3D generation. 

Garbage in, garbage out

The decision to not scrape the internet also gives Adobe an edge in content moderation. Generative AI is notoriously difficult to control, and developers themselves don’t know why the models generate the images and texts they do. Generative AI models have put out questionable and toxic content in numerous cases. 

That all comes down to what it has been trained on, Greenfield says. He says Adobe’s model has never seen a picture of Joe Biden or Donald Trump, for example, and it cannot be coaxed into generating political misinformation. The AI model’s training data has no news content or famous people. It has not been trained on any copyrighted material, such as images of Mickey Mouse. 

“It just doesn’t understand what that concept is,” says Greenfield. 

Adobe also applies automated content moderation at the point of creation to check that Firefly’s creations are safe for professional use. The model is prohibited from creating news stories or violent images. Some names of artists are also blocked. Firefly-generated content comes with labels that indicate it has been created using AI, and the image’s edit history. 

During a critical election year, the need to know who made a piece of content, and how, is especially important. Adobe has been a vocal advocate for labels on AI content that tell where it originated, and with whom. 

The company started the Content Authenticity Initiative, an association promoting the use of labels which tell you whether content is AI-generated or not, along with the New York Times and Twitter (now X). The initiative now has over 2,500 members. It is also part of developing C2PA, an industry standard label which shows where a piece of content has come from, and how it was created. 

“We’re long overdue [for] a better education in media literacy and tools that support people’s ability to validate any content that claims to represent reality,” Greenfield says. 

Adobe’s approach highlights the need for AI companies to be thinking deeply about content moderation, says Claire Leibowicz, head of AI and media integrity at the nonprofit Partnership on AI. 

Adobe’s approach toward generative AI serves those societal goals by fighting misinformation as well as promoting business goals, such as preserving creator autonomy and attribution, adds Leibowicz. 

“The business mission of Adobe is not to prevent misinformation, per se,” she says. “It’s to empower creators. And isn’t this a really elegant confluence of mission and tactics, to be able to kill two birds with one stone?” 

Wadhwani agrees. The company says Firefly-powered features are among its most popular, and 90% of Firefly’s web app users are entirely new customers to Adobe. 

 “I think our approach has definitely been good for business,” Wadhwani says.

Correction: An earlier version of this article had David Wadhwani’s title wrong. This has been amended.

text:
Microsoft’s newly published patent for a "distributed GPU computing network" has many people asking: Isn't this literally what Pi Network is already doing?

On the surface, both tell the same story: pooling idle consumer hardware worldwide to build a decentralized AI compute network. 
Under the hood, however, they are playing two completely different games 👇

1️⃣ Hardware Core: Heavyweight GPUs vs. Lightweight CPUs
🔹 Microsoft Patent: Targets dedicated GPUs inside gaming PCs and laptops. It breaks down massive AI model training into smaller chunks, relying on raw parallel computing power.
🔹 Pi Network: Mobile users simply tap daily for consensus, while desktop Pi Nodes run Docker-based CPU containers for network validation and lightweight AI inference (like basic image recognition)—nowhere near the compute scale of training large models.

2️⃣ Business Loop: B2B Fiat Payouts vs. Web3 Tokenomics
🔹 Microsoft (Web2 Giant): Backed by Azure’s massive enterprise clientele, compute demand is real and immediate. Users contribute GPU power and get paid directly in cash or cloud credits.
🔹 Pi (Web3 / DePIN): Relies on native token incentives, meaning real-world value depends heavily on secondary market liquidity and external demand.

3️⃣ Security Moat: Enterprise Sandboxing vs. Public Networks
Companies won't train proprietary models on consumer PCs without ironclad privacy. A major focus of Microsoft's patent is cryptographic isolation and sandboxing to protect sensitive corporate data—the exact assurance needed to land enterprise deals.

💡 Takeaway:
Similar vision, vastly different scale. A tech giant entering this space validates "distributed compute" as a major future trend and reinforces the broader narrative for the sector.

⚠️ Scam Alert: This is strictly a patent filing—Microsoft has NOT released any official GPU mining or earning app. Any link claiming to offer "official Microsoft GPU mining" right now is 100% malware/scam. Stay safe!

Where do you see distributed AI compute heading? Will Web2 giants dominate, or will Web3 DePIN projects take the lead? 👇

text:
One of the group struggled at first with the classic human reflex: the need to manage, to stay in control, to analyze instead of surrender. We stayed close, offering only the lightest verbal anchors. Each time he edged closer to release, the medicine met him with patience rather than force. Slowly the grip loosened. Eventually he dropped fully, and the relief that followed was almost audible in the room.
Another carried a long habit of emotional control. The medicine did not negotiate. It met him face-to-face, and the confrontation was honest. He purged—clean, purposeful, necessary—and on the other side of that release found a state of pure experiencing that required no commentary, no defense, no story. Just presence.
Throughout both the morning and afternoon sessions, the lasers remained available as an optional doorway into the particular visual phenomena Goler and others have described—the recurring geometric structures and code-like symbols that appear within the diffracted light. Some chose to engage that exploration; others remained fully immersed in the inner landscapes the medicine itself presented. Either way, the container stayed the same: careful, non-directive, and devoted entirely to personal discovery.
What became clear, again, is that deep medicine is not always about receiving concise answers, tidy information, or clear instruction from the other side. Sometimes the molecule seems to laugh at our direct questions. It refuses to hand over a neat download and instead points us back toward the slower, more ordinary work of connecting—with ourselves, with one another, with the texture of daily life—and discovering the answers that can only be found by living them. The real gift is often the capacity it restores: the ability to listen inward, to trust what arises in the quiet of terrestrial experience, and to keep doing the work long after the session ends.
In the end, the depth of any such journey remains profoundly subjective. No one standing outside it can measure its value or declare its meaning. Only the one who walked it can know what it offered, what it asked, and what it ultimately revealed.
The room itself seemed to breathe with them. Connection moved in every direction: connection to self, yes, but also to the people sharing the space, to the quiet clink of a water glass later, to the cultural threads each person carried, to the shifting perceptions that make ordinary reality feel newly transparent. Psychedelic medicines have a way of dissolving the usual filters so that understanding can arrive not as theory but as direct knowing. In scientific language we might speak of temporary shifts in default-mode network activity, increased neural entropy, or enhanced binding of serotonin receptors. In the language of the experience itself, it simply feels like the universe deciding to show you a few more of its cards—and then sitting with you while you decide what to do with them.
We were not offering therapy that day. We were offering a carefully held container for people who already knew how to meet themselves. The medicine did the rest. And when the final session softened and the gongs spoke one last time, the seven of us remained for a while in the quiet afterglow—feet still pointed toward the center, hearts a little more open than when we had begun.

text:
Your distinction between “Islam” and “Muslims” is the standard defensive move, but it does not hold up well against the primary sources or the historical record. The Quran, Hadith, and classical jurisprudence do not merely tolerate conquest, slavery, and subordination of non-Muslims as unfortunate human failings; they regulate and in important respects endorse them.

The early expansions that created what became the Arab world were military campaigns framed as jihad. Non-Muslims were typically offered conversion, the jizya (a poll tax imposed on the subjugated while they remained in a state of “humiliation,” per Quran 9:29 and the classical commentaries), or the sword. Captives were enslaved as a matter of course. This is not an external “political” overlay; it is how the tradition itself describes the process. The same sources that praise freeing slaves as a meritorious act (and they do) also permit ownership, sexual use of female captives, and the buying and selling of human beings. Muhammad owned slaves and took captives as wives/concubines. Manumission as piety is not the same as abolition of the institution.
The Arab/Muslim slave trade operated for roughly thirteen centuries—far longer than the Atlantic trade—and estimates put the numbers of Africans alone in the multi-millions (commonly cited ranges of 10–17 million, plus Europeans and others). It was suppressed in large part by British naval power in the 19th century, after Britain had already moved against its own earlier involvement in the Atlantic trade. That fact does not vanish because the British Empire also had colonial sins. Pointing at British or American history is whataboutism; it does not rewrite the Islamic legal and historical record on slavery or conquest. Slavery has not disappeared in every Muslim-majority society either. 

Hereditary slavery persists in Mauritania among Arab-Berber and other communities; trafficking and forced labour continue in places such as Libya. These are not fringe anomalies unrelated to long-standing social patterns.
On the double-standard point: yes, Christians and Jews have done terrible things, and Christian societies eventually generated strong internal abolitionist movements that successfully argued against practices that had biblical precedents. Islam has not produced an equivalent successful doctrinal reformation that removes the permission for jihadist expansion, the classical rules on dhimmis, or the permissibility of slavery. Large majorities in many Muslim-majority countries still want some form of sharia as official or influential law. 

Derived figures from the 2013 Pew survey show substantial support (often majorities or large minorities in places such as Egypt, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Jordan, and the Palestinian territories) for the death penalty for apostasy among those who favour sharia, and non-trivial minorities for hudud corporal punishments. Support for violence “in defence of Islam” has declined from earlier peaks in many places but remains double-digit in several countries and territories.

text:
⛵ CHRISTOPHER COLUMBUS: THE VOYAGES THAT CHANGED THE WORLD, IN 250 FACTS

🧭 BEFORE THE VOYAGE
𝟏. Christopher Columbus was born in Genoa, Italy, probably in 1451

𝟐. In Italian he was Cristoforo Colombo, and in Spain Cristóbal Colón

𝟑. His father Domenico was a wool weaver

𝟒. He went to sea as a teenager, trading around the Mediterranean

𝟓. In 1476 his ship was sunk in a battle off Portugal, and he swam ashore, reportedly clinging to an oar

𝟔. He settled in Lisbon, where his brother Bartholomew worked as a mapmaker

𝟕. He sailed as far north as Ireland and, he claimed, Iceland

𝟖. He also sailed south to the Portuguese fort of Elmina on Africa's Gold Coast

𝟗. Around 1479 he married Filipa Moniz Perestrelo, from a noble family linked to the Madeira islands

𝟏𝟎. Their son Diego was born around 1480

𝟏𝟏. He read Marco Polo's travels and filled his books with notes about the riches of Asia

𝟏𝟐. Like all educated Europeans of his day, he knew the Earth was round. The "flat Earth" story is a myth

𝟏𝟑. His real mistake was size: he thought Japan lay about 4,000 km west of the Canary Islands. The true distance is nearly 20,000 km

𝟏𝟒. He was encouraged by a letter and map from the Florentine scholar Toscanelli

𝟏𝟓. Around 1485 King John II of Portugal turned his plan down on his experts' advice

𝟏𝟔. After Filipa died, he moved to Spain with young Diego

𝟏𝟕. Friars at the monastery of La Rábida, near the port of Palos, took them in and backed his plan

𝟏𝟖. In 1486 he first pitched his idea to Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand

𝟏𝟗. A royal commission rejected it, saying his distances were wrong. They were right

𝟐𝟎. While he waited, the Crown paid him a small allowance

𝟐𝟏. In 1488 his second son, Fernando, was born to Beatriz Enríquez de Arana

𝟐𝟐. His brother Bartholomew tried to win backing from the kings of England and France

𝟐𝟑. Columbus waited about six years for a Spanish yes

𝟐𝟒. In January 1492 Spain captured Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Iberia, freeing the monarchs to look further afield

𝟐𝟓. Rejected once more, Columbus rode away, but a royal messenger caught up with him and called him back

𝟐𝟔. The royal treasurer Luis de Santángel persuaded the Queen and helped raise the money

𝟐𝟕. The famous story that Isabella pawned her jewels to pay for the voyage is a myth

𝟐𝟖. On 17 April 1492 the Capitulations of Santa Fe made him "Admiral of the Ocean Sea" and viceroy of any lands he found

𝟐𝟗. He was also promised 10% of all the riches from those lands

𝟑𝟎. The town of Palos was ordered to provide two ships as a punishment for an offence against the Crown

𝟑𝟏. The respected Pinzón brothers, Martín Alonso and Vicente Yáñez, persuaded local sailors to sign up

⛵ THE FIRST VOYAGE (1492–1493)
𝟑𝟐. Three ships set out: the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña

𝟑𝟑. The Santa María was a heavy cargo ship, while the Pinta and Niña were fast, light caravels

𝟑𝟒. The Niña's real name was the Santa Clara. "Niña" was a nickname from her owner, Juan Niño

𝟑𝟓. The Santa María belonged to Juan de la Cosa, who later drew the oldest surviving map showing the Americas

𝟑𝟔. Martín Alonso Pinzón captained the Pinta, and his brother Vicente Yáñez the Niña

𝟑𝟕. About 90 men sailed, almost all experienced sailors from southern Spain

𝟑𝟖. Only four were convicts, pardoned in exchange for joining

𝟑𝟗. An interpreter, Luis de Torres, who spoke Hebrew and Arabic, came along to talk to the "Great Khan" of China

𝟒𝟎. There was no priest on board

𝟒𝟏. They sailed from Palos at dawn on 3 August 1492

𝟒𝟐. Days earlier, the deadline for Spain's Jews to convert or leave the country had expired

𝟒𝟑. Their first stop was the Canary Islands, Spain's last outpost in the Atlantic

𝟒𝟒. The Pinta's rudder broke soon after leaving, and Columbus suspected her owners of sabotage

𝟒𝟓. In the Canaries, the Niña's triangular sails were swapped for square ones to run before the wind

𝟒𝟔. They took on water, firewood and food on the island of La Gomera

𝟒𝟕. On 6 September 1492 they left La Gomera and sailed into the unknown

𝟒𝟖. Columbus kept two logs: a secret true one, and one with shorter distances to stop the crew panicking about how far from home they were

𝟒𝟗. Ironically, the "fake" figures were closer to the truth, because he overestimated his speed

𝟓𝟎. The steady trade winds pushed them west day after day

𝟓𝟏. On 13 September the compass needles drifted from the North Star, alarming the pilots

𝟓𝟐. On 15 September a great meteor fell into the sea

𝟓𝟑. Later in September they entered the Sargasso Sea, so full of floating seaweed that sailors feared running aground

𝟓𝟒. Birds, seaweed and whales raised false hopes of land again and again

𝟓𝟓. On 25 September Martín Alonso Pinzón shouted "Land!" The crew sang a hymn, but it was only clouds

𝟓𝟔. By early October the crew was close to mutiny

𝟓𝟕. On 7 October Columbus changed course to the west-southwest, following flocks of migrating birds

𝟓𝟖. On 10 October, according to some accounts, he promised to turn back if land was not found within days

𝟓𝟗. On 11 October they fished out a carved stick and a branch with berries

𝟔𝟎. That night Columbus said he saw a light "like a small wax candle" rising and falling in the distance

𝟔𝟏. At about 2 a.m. on 12 October 1492, Rodrigo de Triana, a lookout on the Pinta, cried "¡Tierra!"

𝟔𝟐. The Crown had promised a pension of 10,000 maravedís a year to the first to see land

𝟔𝟑. Columbus kept the reward himself, claiming he had seen the light first

𝟔𝟒. The crossing from the Canaries had taken about five weeks

𝟔𝟓. They landed on an island in the Bahamas that its Taíno people called Guanahani

𝟔𝟔. Columbus renamed it San Salvador, "Holy Saviour"

𝟔𝟕. Exactly which island it was is still debated. In 1925 the Bahamas renamed Watling Island as San Salvador

𝟔𝟖. He went ashore with the royal banner and claimed the island for Spain

𝟔𝟗. The Taíno greeted them peacefully, offering parrots, balls of cotton thread and spears

𝟕𝟎. In his log Columbus wrote that they would make good servants and could easily be converted

𝟕𝟏. He saw small gold rings in their noses and asked where the gold came from

𝟕𝟐. He took several Taíno captive to guide him through the islands

𝟕𝟑. He called the people "Indians" because he believed he had reached the Indies

𝟕𝟒. On 28 October he reached Cuba, which he believed was part of mainland Asia

𝟕𝟓. He sent Luis de Torres and another man inland to find the Great Khan. They found a village of thatched huts

𝟕𝟔. There the envoys saw people smoking rolled leaves: Europeans' first meeting with tobacco

𝟕𝟕. The Spaniards also saw people sleeping in hammocks. The word comes from the Taíno language

𝟕𝟖. On 21 November Martín Alonso Pinzón sailed off in the Pinta without permission to hunt for gold

𝟕𝟗. On 6 December Columbus reached a large island he named La Española: Hispaniola

𝟖𝟎. There he met the Taíno chief Guacanagarí, who became his ally

𝟖𝟏. On Christmas Eve 1492, while Columbus slept, a ship's boy at the helm ran the Santa María onto a reef

𝟖𝟐. Guacanagarí's people helped unload the cargo, and Columbus noted that not a single item went missing

𝟖𝟑. From the wreck's timbers the men built a fort, La Navidad, "Christmas"

𝟖𝟒. Columbus left 39 men there: the first European settlement in the Americas since the Vikings

𝟖𝟓. On 4 January 1493 he set sail for home in the Niña

𝟖𝟔. Two days later the Pinta rejoined him. Pinzón had found gold

𝟖𝟕. On 13 January, in a bay on Hispaniola, the Spaniards fought Indigenous archers. Columbus named it the Bay of Arrows

𝟖𝟖. He carried several Taíno captives back to Spain

𝟖𝟗. On 14 February 1493 a violent storm separated the two ships

𝟗𝟎. Sure he would die, Columbus wrote an account of his discovery, sealed it in a barrel and threw it into the sea. It was never found

𝟗𝟏. The crew drew lots with chickpeas, one marked with a cross, to choose who would make a pilgrimage if they survived. Columbus drew the cross

𝟗𝟐. They reached the Azores, where Portuguese officials arrested half the crew as they went ashore to pray

𝟗𝟑. Another storm forced Columbus into Lisbon, the capital of Spain's great rival, on 4 March 1493

𝟗𝟒. King John II of Portugal received him and claimed the new lands might be his

𝟗𝟓. On 15 March 1493 the Niña sailed into Palos, and the Pinta arrived on the very same day

𝟗𝟔. Martín Alonso Pinzón died within weeks, sick and exhausted

𝟗𝟕. Columbus's letter describing his discovery was printed and spread across Europe within months

𝟗𝟖. In Barcelona Isabella and Ferdinand received him as a hero

𝟗𝟗. He paraded Taíno people, parrots and gold before the court

𝟏𝟎𝟎. Six of the Taíno were baptised, with the King and Queen as godparents

𝟏𝟎𝟏. The famous "egg of Columbus" story, in which he makes an egg stand by cracking its end, is probably a legend

𝟏𝟎𝟐. In May 1493 Pope Alexander VI drew a line through the Atlantic, giving lands to its west to Spain

𝟏𝟎𝟑. In 1494 the Treaty of Tordesillas moved the line further west. That is why Brazil speaks Portuguese today

🏝️ THE SECOND VOYAGE (1493–1496)
𝟏𝟎𝟒. This time he sailed with 17 ships and about 1,200 men

𝟏𝟎𝟓. It was a colonising fleet, carrying settlers, soldiers, priests and craftsmen

𝟏𝟎𝟔. The ships carried horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, wheat and sugar cane, which would transform the Americas

𝟏𝟎𝟕. They left Cádiz on 25 September 1493

𝟏𝟎𝟖. The crossing from the Canaries took only about three weeks

𝟏𝟎𝟗. On 3 November 1493 he sighted an island he named Dominica, because it was a Sunday

𝟏𝟏𝟎. He named Guadeloupe after a famous monastery in Spain

𝟏𝟏𝟏. On Guadeloupe the Spaniards reported finding signs of cannibalism among the Carib people

𝟏𝟏𝟐. The word "cannibal" comes from Carib, the name Europeans gave these islanders

𝟏𝟏𝟑. Sailing north, he named Montserrat, Antigua and many other islands

𝟏𝟏𝟒. At St Croix, Spaniards and Caribs fought the first recorded battle between Europeans and Indigenous people in the Caribbean

𝟏𝟏𝟓. He named the Virgin Islands after Saint Ursula and her legendary 11,000 virgins

𝟏𝟏𝟔. On 19 November 1493 he reached Puerto Rico, which he called San Juan Bautista

𝟏𝟏𝟕. On 28 November he reached La Navidad and found it burned to the ground

𝟏𝟏𝟖. All 39 men he had left behind were dead

𝟏𝟏𝟗. The Taíno said the settlers had fought among themselves over gold and women and were killed by the chief Caonabo

𝟏𝟐𝟎. In January 1494 Columbus founded La Isabela on Hispaniola, the first planned European town in the Americas

𝟏𝟐𝟏. Soon after, the first recorded Catholic Mass in the Americas was held there

𝟏𝟐𝟐. The settlers fell ill with fevers, and many died

𝟏𝟐𝟑. Columbus sent 12 ships home, begging Spain for food and medicine

𝟏𝟐𝟒. He sent soldiers inland to the Cibao valley to find gold and built a fort there

𝟏𝟐𝟓. In April 1494 he set off to explore Cuba and Jamaica

𝟏𝟐𝟔. In May 1494 he reached Jamaica, which he called Santiago

𝟏𝟐𝟕. Sailing along Cuba's south coast, he made his crew swear an oath that Cuba was a continent, not an island

𝟏𝟐𝟖. Anyone who later said otherwise faced a fine, and sailors were threatened with having their tongues cut out

𝟏𝟐𝟗. Returning exhausted, he fell gravely ill and was unconscious for days

𝟏𝟑𝟎. His brother Bartholomew arrived on Hispaniola to help him rule

𝟏𝟑𝟏. The settlers' raids for food, gold and women drove the Taíno to revolt

𝟏𝟑𝟐. In 1495 Spanish soldiers with horses and war dogs crushed a Taíno army in the Vega Real valley

𝟏𝟑𝟑. Columbus imposed a tribute: every Taíno over 14 had to hand over a small bell full of gold dust every three months

𝟏𝟑𝟒. Those who failed faced harsh punishment

𝟏𝟑𝟓. In 1495 he shipped about 500 Taíno to Spain as slaves. Some 200 died on the voyage

𝟏𝟑𝟔. Queen Isabella later questioned the trade and ordered some of the enslaved Taíno freed and sent home

𝟏𝟑𝟕. The chief Caonabo was captured, reportedly tricked into wearing shiny handcuffs as if they were royal bracelets. He died on the way to Spain

𝟏𝟑𝟖. In 1495 a hurricane wrecked ships in La Isabela's harbour, one of the first hurricanes recorded by Europeans

𝟏𝟑𝟗. The word "hurricane" comes from the Taíno word hurakán

𝟏𝟒𝟎. From the wrecks the Spaniards built the India, the first European ship built in the Americas

𝟏𝟒𝟏. Complaints about Columbus's rule reached Spain, and the Crown sent an investigator, Juan Aguado

𝟏𝟒𝟐. In March 1496 Columbus sailed home to defend himself, leaving Bartholomew in charge

𝟏𝟒𝟑. Food ran so low on the way home that, according to his son, some sailors proposed eating the Taíno captives. Columbus refused

𝟏𝟒𝟒. In June 1496 he reached Cádiz wearing the plain brown habit of a Franciscan friar

𝟏𝟒𝟓. His brother Bartholomew founded Santo Domingo, now the oldest European-founded city still standing in the Americas

🌊 THE THIRD VOYAGE (1498–1500)
𝟏𝟒𝟔. It took two years to raise money and men for a third voyage

𝟏𝟒𝟕. Few volunteers wanted to go, so convicts were offered pardons to join

𝟏𝟒𝟖. On 30 May 1498 he sailed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda with six ships

𝟏𝟒𝟗. He sent three ships straight to Hispaniola and took the other three further south than ever before

𝟏𝟓𝟎. Near the equator the wind died, and the heat was so fierce that the food and wine spoiled

𝟏𝟓𝟏. On 31 July 1498 a sailor spotted three peaks, and Columbus named the island Trinidad, after the Holy Trinity

𝟏𝟓𝟐. On 1 August 1498 he saw the coast of South America for the first time

𝟏𝟓𝟑. On 5 August his men landed on the Paria peninsula in Venezuela. Columbus, suffering from an eye infection, stayed on board

𝟏𝟓𝟒. It was the first recorded European landing on the South American mainland

𝟏𝟓𝟓. He saw the Orinoco River pour so much fresh water into the sea that it must drain "a very great continent"

𝟏𝟓𝟔. He wrote that it was "another world", yet he still believed it lay near Asia

𝟏𝟓𝟕. He even suggested the Garden of Eden lay nearby

𝟏𝟓𝟖. He also claimed the Earth was not a perfect sphere but shaped like a pear

𝟏𝟓𝟗. He named the dangerous straits around Trinidad the Serpent's Mouth and the Dragon's Mouth

𝟏𝟔𝟎. Half-blind and crippled by arthritis, he headed for Hispaniola

𝟏𝟔𝟏. On 31 August 1498 he reached Santo Domingo

𝟏𝟔𝟐. He found the colony in open revolt, led by the former mayor Francisco Roldán

𝟏𝟔𝟑. To make peace, he gave the rebels land and the forced labour of Indigenous people

𝟏𝟔𝟒. He also had several rebels hanged

𝟏𝟔𝟓. Settlers who returned to Spain complained bitterly about the Columbus brothers

𝟏𝟔𝟔. In 1500 the Crown sent a new judge, Francisco de Bobadilla, with full powers

𝟏𝟔𝟕. When Bobadilla arrived in August 1500, Spaniards' bodies were hanging from the gallows

𝟏𝟔𝟖. He arrested Columbus and his brothers

𝟏𝟔𝟗. In October 1500 Columbus was sent back to Spain in chains

𝟏𝟕𝟎. The ship's captain offered to remove the chains, but Columbus refused until the King and Queen ordered it

𝟏𝟕𝟏. According to his son, he kept the chains for the rest of his life and wanted to be buried with them

𝟏𝟕𝟐. In 2006 historians publicised Bobadilla's long-lost report, full of witness accounts of the brothers' brutal rule

𝟏𝟕𝟑. In December 1500 the monarchs freed him and received him at the Alhambra in Granada

𝟏𝟕𝟒. They restored his wealth, but not his power as governor

𝟏𝟕𝟓. Nicolás de Ovando was sent to govern Hispaniola in his place

𝟏𝟕𝟔. Meanwhile Portugal's Vasco da Gama had reached India by sailing around Africa in 1498

𝟏𝟕𝟕. In 1500 the Portuguese explorer Cabral landed in Brazil

𝟏𝟕𝟖. Amerigo Vespucci, who sailed along South America, argued it was a "New World"

𝟏𝟕𝟗. In 1507 a German map named the new continent "America" after Vespucci, not Columbus

𝟏𝟖𝟎. Back in Spain, Columbus wrote a Book of Prophecies, arguing his voyages fulfilled the Bible

⚓ THE FOURTH VOYAGE (1502–1504)
𝟏𝟖𝟏. He called his last journey "the High Voyage"

𝟏𝟖𝟐. His goal was to find a sea passage through the new lands to the Indian Ocean

𝟏𝟖𝟑. On 11 May 1502 he left Cádiz with four ships and about 140 men

𝟏𝟖𝟒. His 13-year-old son Fernando sailed with him

𝟏𝟖𝟓. He was forbidden to stop at Hispaniola

𝟏𝟖𝟔. The crossing took just 21 days, his fastest ever

𝟏𝟖𝟕. In June 1502 he anchored off Santo Domingo anyway, warned that a hurricane was coming and asked for shelter

𝟏𝟖𝟖. Governor Ovando refused to let him in and ignored his warning

𝟏𝟖𝟗. A treasure fleet of about 30 ships sailed for Spain anyway

𝟏𝟗𝟎. The hurricane sank around 20 of them, drowning some 500 men, including Bobadilla and the rebel Roldán

𝟏𝟗𝟏. The one ship that reached Spain carried Columbus's own share of the gold

𝟏𝟗𝟐. His own ships, sheltering in a nearby bay, survived

𝟏𝟗𝟑. In July 1502 he reached the island of Guanaja off Honduras

𝟏𝟗𝟒. There he met a huge trading canoe, as long as a galley and about 2.4 m wide, with some 25 paddlers

𝟏𝟗𝟓. It carried cotton cloth, copper tools and cacao beans, probably from the Maya world

𝟏𝟗𝟔. The traders treated cacao beans as money: when some were dropped, his son wrote, they stooped to pick them up as if they had lost their eyes

𝟏𝟗𝟕. For about a month he battled east along the coast of Honduras against wind, rain and current

𝟏𝟗𝟖. When the coast finally turned south, he named the point Cape Gracias a Dios: "Thanks be to God"

𝟏𝟗𝟗. He sailed on along the coasts of Nicaragua and Costa Rica

𝟐𝟎𝟎. Local people told him of another sea just a few days' walk away. It was the Pacific

𝟐𝟎𝟏. He never found a way through, unaware how close the Pacific was

𝟐𝟎𝟐. Off Panama he found gold and heard of rich mines in Veragua

𝟐𝟎𝟑. Around Christmas 1502 savage storms hit the fleet, and a waterspout passed close by. Columbus read from the Gospel of John to ward it off

𝟐𝟎𝟒. In January 1503 he founded Santa María de Belén in Panama, the first attempted European settlement on the American mainland

𝟐𝟎𝟓. The local chief, Quibián, attacked, and the settlement was abandoned in April 1503

𝟐𝟎𝟔. Feverish and alone, Columbus wrote that he heard a heavenly voice comforting him

𝟐𝟎𝟕. Shipworms had riddled the hulls with holes, and two ships had to be abandoned

𝟐𝟎𝟖. With two leaking ships left, he tried to reach Hispaniola but could not

𝟐𝟎𝟗. On 25 June 1503 he ran both ships aground on Jamaica's north coast

𝟐𝟏𝟎. He and his men were stranded there for a year

𝟐𝟏𝟏. His loyal officer Diego Méndez paddled a dugout canoe across open sea to Hispaniola to fetch help

𝟐𝟏𝟐. Some of the Taíno paddlers died of thirst on the crossing

𝟐𝟏𝟑. Governor Ovando left Columbus stranded for months before sending a rescue ship

𝟐𝟏𝟒. In January 1504 about half the men mutinied under the Porras brothers and set off on their own

𝟐𝟏𝟓. The local Taíno grew tired of feeding the Spaniards and stopped bringing food

𝟐𝟏𝟔. Columbus had an almanac predicting a total lunar eclipse on 29 February 1504

𝟐𝟏𝟕. He told the Taíno chiefs that God was angry and would make the moon "inflamed with wrath"

𝟐𝟏𝟖. When the moon turned blood red, the terrified Taíno begged him to intercede, and the food came back

𝟐𝟏𝟗. In May 1504 his loyal men, led by his brother Bartholomew, defeated the mutineers

𝟐𝟐𝟎. In June 1504 a rescue ship finally arrived

𝟐𝟐𝟏. On 7 November 1504 he reached Spain. He never sailed again

⚰️ HIS LAST YEARS AND LEGACY
𝟐𝟐𝟐. On 26 November 1504 Queen Isabella, his greatest supporter, died

𝟐𝟐𝟑. He spent his final months begging King Ferdinand to restore his titles and income

𝟐𝟐𝟒. Contrary to legend, he did not die poor. He lived comfortably on his share of the gold

𝟐𝟐𝟓. He died in Valladolid, Spain, on 20 May 1506, aged about 54

𝟐𝟐𝟔. Most historians believe he died still convinced he had reached Asia

𝟐𝟐𝟕. His remains travelled further after death than many people do in life: Valladolid, Seville, Santo Domingo, Havana and back to Seville

𝟐𝟐𝟖. The Dominican Republic still says it holds his bones in a giant monument in Santo Domingo

𝟐𝟐𝟗. DNA tests show at least some of the remains in Seville Cathedral are his

𝟐𝟑𝟎. In 2024 a Spanish documentary claimed DNA showed he was of Sephardic Jewish origin. Other scientists disputed it

𝟐𝟑𝟏. His son Diego later became governor of Hispaniola

𝟐𝟑𝟐. His son Fernando built one of Europe's largest libraries, with more than 15,000 books

𝟐𝟑𝟑. Fernando also wrote a biography of his father

𝟐𝟑𝟒. The original log of the first voyage is lost. We know it from a summary by the friar Bartolomé de las Casas

𝟐𝟑𝟓. Las Casas also became one of the fiercest critics of how the Spanish treated Indigenous people

𝟐𝟑𝟔. His heirs fought the Spanish Crown in court over his rights for decades

𝟐𝟑𝟕. Within decades of his arrival, Hispaniola's Taíno population collapsed from disease, war and forced labour

𝟐𝟑𝟖. The swap of plants, animals and diseases that followed is known as the Columbian Exchange

𝟐𝟑𝟗. Europe gained maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, cacao and tobacco

𝟐𝟒𝟎. The Americas gained horses, cattle, pigs, wheat and sugar cane, and also smallpox and measles

𝟐𝟒𝟏. He was not the first European to reach the Americas: Norse sailors reached Newfoundland about 500 years earlier

𝟐𝟒𝟐. He never set foot on the mainland of what is now the United States

𝟐𝟒𝟑. He crossed the Atlantic eight times in all

𝟐𝟒𝟒. No trace of the Santa María has ever been found. A 2014 claim to have found the wreck was rejected by UNESCO experts

𝟐𝟒𝟓. Colombia, British Columbia and Columbus, Ohio, are all named after him

𝟐𝟒𝟔. Columbus Day became a US national holiday in 1937

𝟐𝟒𝟕. Spain celebrates its National Day on 12 October, the day of his landfall

𝟐𝟒𝟖. Many places now mark Indigenous Peoples' Day instead of Columbus Day

𝟐𝟒𝟗. In 2020 several statues of him were toppled or removed in US cities

𝟐𝟓𝟎. More than 500 years on, his voyages are seen as the start of both globalisation and centuries of colonial conquest

text:
My cousin works in the front office of a professional baseball team in Japan.

Every season, the team evaluates its foreign players on a standard form. Eight categories. The form was designed in 1987 and has never been changed. It was built to answer one question: will this American cause problems?

This year's American is a catcher from Oklahoma. Thirty-three. Slightly wider than our dugout door. Let's call him Lane.

My cousin let me translate his form.

1. PUNCTUALITY
Arrives two hours before every game. Not to train. To learn the names of the stadium staff. All 140 of them. He knows the parking attendant's daughter is applying to nursing school. We did not know this.

2. RESPECT FOR SENIORITY
Calls the 68-year-old groundskeeper "Mr. Enomoto, sir." Calls the team owner "Chief." Calls the owner's 91-year-old mother "young lady." She has attended every home game since.

3. TEAM HARMONY
Started a barbecue in the players' parking lot after every home win. Our backup shortstop, 22, has not spoken in a team meeting in three seasons. He now runs the grill. He has opinions about ribs. He shares them.

4. EMOTIONAL RESTRAINT
In August, our rookie hit his first walk-off home run. The first player out of the dugout was Lane. Crying. He was not involved in the play. He was involved emotionally.

5. LANGUAGE EFFORT
Speaks 41 words of Japanese. 30 are food. Says "arigato" to the umpire after strike three. The umpires held a meeting about this. They have decided they like it.

6. FAN RELATIONS
Signs every autograph. Every single one. After a loss in July, he stayed two hours in the rain. A security guard held an umbrella over him. A second guard held an umbrella over the first guard. A third guard went for coffee.

7. CONDUCT TOWARD OPPONENTS
Tipped his cap to a pitcher who struck him out. The pitcher's mother wrote us a letter. We have no procedure for this letter. It is in a drawer.

8. ADDITIONAL REMARKS
Our rookie is Kaisei. He is 20. His father had not missed a home game since Kaisei signed. Three hours each way. Section 14, row 3. He always brought the same banner, made from an old tablecloth, with Kaisei's name painted on it in big, shaky letters.

In June, his father died suddenly.

Lane does not understand Buddhist funerals. He went anyway. He bought a black suit that morning. It was the biggest one in the store, and it was still too small. He took the last seat in the last row.

When it was his turn to offer incense, he froze. He didn't know how.

Kaisei's little brother, who is nine, came down the aisle to the last row, took Lane's huge hand, and showed him. Pinch. Lift to the forehead. Drop. Bow.

Lane did it exactly the way he was taught. Then he stayed for all three hours.

At the end, he gave Kaisei his bat. The one he hit his first home run in Japan with.

"Your dad's got a better view than any of us now," he said. "Every at-bat. Let's give him something to watch."

The next home game, there was something new hanging in our dugout. An old tablecloth. Kaisei's name in big, shaky letters.

Lane had asked the family if he could borrow it. He hung it himself before every game until the season ended. Nobody told him to.

Kaisei batted .310 from June on. With that bat.

The walk-off in August, the one Lane cried about? That was Kaisei. That was the bat. Rounding third, Kaisei pointed at the dugout. Not at the crowd. At the tablecloth.

The form ends with one last box. RECOMMEND CONTRACT RENEWAL: YES / NO.

For 39 years, the general manager has circled one word and filed it.

This year, somebody turned the form over.

Twenty-eight signatures. The entire roster. The backup shortstop. Kaisei, in very large letters. Mr. Enomoto, the groundskeeper, who is not on the roster and was not asked. A very careful pencil signature from a nine-year-old, who is also not on the roster. And Kaisei's mother, who mailed hers in a separate envelope and asked that it please be stapled on.

Under all of them, one word in English, in the groundskeeper's handwriting:

"PLEASE."

Lane signed for two more years.

text:
XPS5 (RELEASE) 
v1.0.1 is out  X on your PS5, as a real native app. Not a browser, not a web wrapper. Free and open source, built for the controller, and now it updates itself.

🛑Quick note first: XPS5 is unofficial homebrew, not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony or X. It needs a jailbroken PS5. Use it at your own risk: you alone are responsible for your console and your X account.

New in 1.0.1
• Updates inside XPS5: it looks for a new version every time it opens. When one is out, Settings → Updates tells you: press ✕ and it downloads it, checks its size and SHA-256, and installs it

• Updates come over verified HTTPS from the project's GitHub Pages, with no account data and no cookies

What it does
• Your timelines: For you and Following, with pictures, videos, GIFs, quotes, polls, badges and counts. Long posts show in full, and Following remembers where you left off

• Post and reply with the PS5 keyboard: up to 4 screenshots or 1 clip straight from your PS5 captures, polls, quotes and scheduled posts (X Premium)

• Like, repost, bookmark, follow, mute and block, plus the ••• menu as on https://t.co/A9td0tSDT8: delete, pin, and edit (X Premium)

• Explore (trending and news, without promoted items), search, Notifications, Chat (direct messages), Bookmarks, Lists, Scheduled posts, History and Articles

• Up to 5 X accounts on one console

• 7 languages (English, Português, Español, Français, Deutsch, Italiano, Nederlands), following your PS5's language

• Day and Night themes, rendered at your TV's resolution up to 4K. The controller's light bar takes the colour of the banner on screen

Made for your games
• X notifications over your game, as real PS5 notifications with an Open button. You choose how often: every 30 s to 10 min

• It knows what you're playing: the game and its hashtag go into the composer, and that game's captures come first

• Spoiler shield: posts about the game you're playing stay covered until you open them

• New screenshot or trophy? XPS5 offers to post it on X

• It tells you when one of your posts is taking off

• Playing now: see which people you follow are playing, and what. Turn it on and your X profile shows your game too

• Grok hints without spoilers for the game you're playing

• Videos in the sharpest MP4 X has, with sound

• Made for the controller: the left stick moves a pointer, the right stick scrolls, and every button has a job. R2 likes, L2 replies, Options writes a new post, PS takes you back to your game

How it works
• 37,860 lines of C in 78 files, plus 9,845 lines of tests. A real native title (TWPS00001) in the Media tab

• Its own renderer: every frame is drawn on the CPU by 3 worker threads (anti-aliased shapes, TrueType text, frosted glass) at your TV's real pixels, then copied in 8×8 tiles straight into the PS5's video out. 1080p, 1440p or 4K

• It talks to X's web endpoints the same way https://t.co/A9td0tSDT8 does, with your own session. No API key, nothing paid

• HTTPS through the PS5's own libSceHttp, always verified. Payloads get no system certificates, so XPS5 brings its own Let's Encrypt roots

• Its own video player: an MP4 reader (progressive and fragmented) with FFmpeg 8.1.3's H.264 and AAC decoders, picture and sound kept in sync

• Your screenshots and clips are read from the console and uploaded to X in parts of up to 4 MiB, the way https://t.co/A9td0tSDT8's composer does it

• Login: X's own login page, in a WebKit build for the PS5 that runs as a separate process and is drawn inside XPS5. It only opens X's pages, and its cookies and cache are wiped when it closes. Your password goes only to X, over HTTPS. XPS5 never keeps it

• A 333 KiB background payload keeps your X notifications coming after XPS5 closes

• Updates: a GitHub Actions workflow publishes each release's installer with its size and SHA-256 on GitHub Pages. XPS5 checks both before the ELF loader ever gets the file

• Privacy: XPS5 only talks to X, plus GitHub Pages for updates. Your sessions and settings stay on your console, and the system log only gets status codes and counts: never your posts, messages or session

• Every module that doesn't need the console is tested on the PC with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer

• GPL-3.0. Every line of the source is on GitHub

Install
• Download https://t.co/I8iff6w29J from GitHub and check SHA256SUMS.txt

• Load your jailbreak and send XPS5.elf to port 9021 with your usual payload sender (on Windows, the included send.ps1 does it)

• Wait for the notification "XPS5 written to /data/homebrew/TWPS00001". The first install also writes the login window (about 144 MiB), so give it a moment

• ShadowMountPlus adds XPS5 to the Media tab in about 15 seconds. Open it, press ✕ on "Log in to X" and sign in on X's own page

• On 1.0.0? Send 1.0.1 the same way, just once. From then on XPS5 updates itself, and your accounts and settings stay

• Uninstalling: send XPS5-uninstall.elf. It removes everything XPS5 wrote. Your captures and your games are not touched

• Good to know: X may ask you to verify your account, or lock it for a while (error 326). If that happens, unlock it at https://t.co/A9td0tSDT8

📝 To-do
• Test more firmware versions
• Invites to play: a DM that opens the game on your friend's PS5 (in testing)
• Send a capture straight into a DM (in testing)
• Sign in with Google and Apple in the login window
• More PSN-style social features on top of X
• Your ideas

!!!Note: not everything has been tested yet, so some bugs are expected. They will be fixed in an upcoming update, and XPS5 will tell you as soon as it's out.!!!

Needs a PS5 on firmware 13.60 with a working jailbreak, ELF loader and ShadowMountPlus.

https://t.co/Y2k5q9fuA3

Feedback and suggestions are welcome, here on X or on GitHub: tell me what works, what breaks and what you want to see next. A repost or a ⭐ on the repo helps XPS5 reach more players.

Next release: BrowserPS5 RN 👀 Follow so you don't miss it.

Have a great weekend, everyone! 🎮

text:
Sunlight glints off New Troy Bay as Metropolis settles intact onto its granite foundations with scarcely a spilled coffee cup—streetcars ringing brass bells along Broadway, tugboats hooting in sudden bewilderment, eight million people blinking up at ordinary white clouds as though waking simultaneously from the same fever dream. Up on the Daily Planet roof, Lois Lane catches Jimmy Olsen's sleeve to steady herself; down on Pier 14, Harbor Police snap steel cuffs around Lex Luthor's wrists beside salvaged wreckage from his submerged East River lab, though nobody notices Luthor press a microscopic, faintly glowing green speck beneath his tongue—a stray fleck of Kryptonite dust shaken loose from Brainiac's hull plates during re-entry, pulsing against Luthor's gums like a secret promise.

Two thousand miles north, where polar winds scour blue glacial cliffs clean of footprints, twin beams of ruby heat carve deep corridors into eternal ice. Working undisturbed beneath dancing green curtains of aurora, Superman hollows out a vaulted sanctuary inside the mountain—the Fortress of Solitude—sealing its massive bronze doors behind an eighty-ton golden arrow-key laid across snowdrifts outside so passing bush pilots mistake it for a weather marker only a hurricane could budge.

Inside the quietest room in the world, mounted upon shock-absorbing alabaster beneath a warm red-spectrum lamp, Kandor glows softly in the twilight. Leaning close to a crystal audio transceiver wired through the stopper, Kal-El speaks quietly in improving Kryptonian to Kim-Da, promising that every spare hour between Earth's emergencies belongs to finding a safe way to make them tall again. For the first time in his memory, perhaps, he doesn't feel entirely alone under the stars.

Monday morning smells of hot lead type, cheap ink, and burnt diner coffee.

Clark Kent pushes clumsily through the Daily Planet bullpen carrying two cardboard coffees, sneezing mildly into a folded handkerchief while Lois Lane hammers forty words a minute into her Underwood, barely glancing up to scoff at how any grown reporter managed to get stuck inside a subway turnstile during the biggest cosmic scoop in human history. Clark sets the hotter cup beside her elbow—extra sugar, just how she likes it though she never told him—offers an apologetic half-smile behind thick horn-rimmed lenses, and looks out past the spinning brass globe toward a clear blue harbor sky.

text:
Metropolis doesn't walk; it stampedes. Elevated trains thunder above canyons of buff limestone and polished chrome, newsboys shout afternoon extras through exhaust haze, and forty stories overhead, a colossal gilded globe turns lazily atop the Daily Planet building like a second sun tethered to Ninth Street.

Up in the twelfth-floor city room, seventy Underwood typewriters hammer out a steady iron rain. Perry White stalks between desks chomping an unlit Panatela cigar down to wet shreds, bellowing for shipping manifests while teenaged copyboy Jimmy Olsen—all freckles, red cowlick, and crooked green bow tie—dodges flying wastebaskets with wet darkroom prints clipped to his sleeve.

Clark Kent fits into the corner desk near the water cooler almost too well. He hunches two inches out of his true height, speaks half an octave softer than necessary, fumbles revolving doors, and lets sharper reporters raid his pencil cup. Lois Lane, seated six feet away in a razor-cut navy pinstripe suit with a tilted felt hat pinned over dark curls, sizes up Perry's new hire in roughly four seconds and writes him off as harmless Kansas wallpaper.

She has bigger game tonight. Two stories, actually, neither of which Perry wants touching libel court without hard proof: at midnight, Evelyn Curry goes to the electric chair at State Penitentiary for a fatal shooting Lois suspects was committed by brassy nightclub singer Claire, and downtown, sleek munitions lobbyist Alex Greer is quietly bribing Senator Barrows to push through an emergency defense contract tied to black-market exotic weaponry.

"Stick to flower shows, Kent," Lois tosses over her shoulder, snatching her handbag as the five-o'clock whistle blows. "Real news bites."

Clark smiles mildly, adjusts his horn-rimmed glasses, waits until the elevator doors slide shut, and steps calmly out the open twelfth-story washroom window into rushing twilight air.

Earth's yellow sun has soaked into him for twenty-four years now; he doesn't merely leap, as he did in Smallville's pastures—he rides Earth's magnetic lines like a hawk on a thermal, crimson cape snapping clean above harbor tugboats.

By ten-thirty, guided by telescanner vision piercing coastal fog, he intercepts Claire packing steamer trunks aboard a Panama-bound freighter at Pier 9. One look at a six-foot-three stranger in primary colors hovering serenely outside her locked brass porthole drains every drop of bravado from her painted lips; within ten minutes she scribbles a seven-page confession naming her accomplices.

At 11:57 PM, cold rain needles the slate roof of the Governor's Mansion.

Down in the foyer, two state troopers whirl as boots thud softly onto the front veranda. When the tall figure in blue and red ignores their barked warning and grasps the two-inch solid steel security door with bare hands, both troopers open fire with Thompson submachine guns.

Lead slugs flatten like dropped nickels against the crimson S across his chest, tinkling harmlessly onto the parquet floor.

He doesn't strike the troopers. He gently plucks both hot barrels from their hands, knots the steel gun-tubes together like wet licorice, peels the reinforced vault door off its hinges to climb the grand staircase, and deposits a bound, spitting Claire—alongside her signed confession—squarely atop the Governor's quilted bedspread with ninety seconds left before the prison dynamo throws its switch. Leaning against the mahogany bedpost with arms folded, he waits politely until the trembling Governor screams Evelyn Curry's stay of execution into the candlestick telephone, then offers a quiet goodnight and blurs out the open French doors.

Crossing the Lower East Side tenements on his way home, his hearing—tuned too wide, perhaps, in the exhilaration of open sky—catches a woman's sharp cry and the ugly snap of cowhide behind a fourth-floor curtain. Glass shatters inward as he lands between a terrified seamstress and her drunken husband. The brute lunges with a pearl-handled switchblade; steel meets bare collarbone and snaps clean in half. One open-handed shove sends the man through a lath-and-plaster partition into his own icebox—alive, unbroken, and permanently cured of lifting a belt—while the stranger pauses only long enough to drape a fallen wool shawl over the wife's shaking shoulders before leaping back into the mist.

By noon the next day, Metropolis talks of nothing else. A circus acrobat? A Martian? A secret New Deal project?

Lois Lane is furious she missed him, which is probably why she lets mild-mannered Clark talk her into dinner at the Chez Pierre supper club that evening—mostly because she knows lobbyist Alex Greer drinks champagne in the back VIP alcove, and Clark makes a convenient decoy. Halfway through the soup course, Greer's chief enforcer, a thick-necked bruiser named Butch Matson who dislikes reporters eyeing his boss's booth, swagger-steps up to their table, blows cigar smoke in Clark's face, and grabs Lois's wrist for a rumba.

Clark puts on a masterclass in cowardice. He stammers, knocks over a breadbasket, apologizes to Matson's cufflinks, and edges backward toward the coatroom while crimson fury rises up Lois's throat.

Lois slaps Matson clean across the jaw herself, flings her linen napkin into Clark's minestrone, and marches out into the rain, swearing she wouldn't cross a puddle on Clark Kent's coat.

She makes it half a block before tires screech against wet cobblestones. An emerald-green sedan jumps the curb; Matson and three gunmen yank Lois off her heels into the backseat, roaring north onto the winding cliffside asphalt of the Palisades Road to dump nosy Miss Lane into the Hudson.

Two miles past the city limits, Matson's high beams slice the fog—and illuminate two scarlet boots planted wide on the double yellow line.

"Run him flat!" Matson barks.

The driver floors it. Eighty miles an hour. Seventy yards. Twenty.

Hands close beneath the chrome front bumper. Metal shrieks like a slaughtered hog as two tons of Detroit steel stop dead, rear wheels spinning wildly in empty air. Inside the cab, Matson's pistol clatters across the dashboard while Lois presses both palms against the cracked safety glass, scarcely breathing. Effortlessly—almost thoughtfully, as though checking the weight of a melon—the caped man lifts the emerald-green sedan clear above his head, tilts it forty degrees until Matson and his three trigger-men spill howling onto the roadside weeds, and brings the empty automobile smashing nose-first down against a granite boulder in a shower of sparks and radiator steam.

Before Matson's crew can scramble past the ditch, strong arms scoop Lois out of the damp grass. For forty dizzying seconds she smells crisp high-altitude ozone and, strangely enough, clean dry hay, watching harbor lights wheel far beneath her heels before he sets her gently beside a streetcar kiosk near Printing House Square.

"Tell Mr. White," says a warm baritone she almost—though surely not—thinks she has heard before, "that Miss Curry is having breakfast at home."

Up he goes, clearing an elevated railway trestle in a single soaring arc. Two hours later, Lois rips her third sheet out of the roller, types SUPERMAN in forty-point headline caps, and hands Perry White the biggest morning edition since Lindbergh.

text:
AN OPEN LETTER TO GEORGE W. BUSH: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS AFTER 9/11, EXPLAIN “ISLAM IS A RELIGION OF PEACE”

THE EVIDENCE™

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

Dear President Bush:

Your administration repeatedly advanced the declaration that “Islam is a religion of peace.” Your press secretary, Ari Fleischer, explicitly identified it as your position. Twenty-five years after September 11, Americans are entitled to ask what justified that sweeping assurance and how you reconcile it with the continuing violence of organizations invoking Islamic authority.

The wording and chronology deserve precision. At the Islamic Center of Washington on September 17, 2001, your exact words were “Islam is peace.” The longer formulation became an expressly stated administration position. This letter addresses that broader declaration, rather than attributing the longer sentence to your September 17 speech.

You were speaking to a wounded country. Americans had watched people leap from burning buildings. Families were searching for loved ones. The nation needed leadership, an accurate explanation of the enemy, and assurance that the government would protect its citizens.

Your mosque visit addressed another immediate concern. You described Muslim women afraid to leave their homes and reminded Americans that their Muslim neighbors included military personnel, physicians, business owners, and parents. You condemned intimidation against innocent people. That was a legitimate exercise of presidential leadership.

But protecting those citizens did not require you to pronounce a definitive judgment on the nature of Islam. You could have defended their rights, condemned retaliation, and insisted on individual accountability without presenting a sweeping religious conclusion as an established fact.

What qualified your administration to settle which interpretation of Islam was authentic?

YOUR DECLARATION LEFT THE CENTRAL QUESTION UNANSWERED

The terrorists claimed religious justification. You rejected their claim. That rejection expressed a moral judgment, but it did not explain how their interpretation developed, why it attracted followers, or how its influence could be defeated.

Those questions were essential. An ideology does not lose its influence because a president declares that its adherents misunderstand their religion. Its arguments must be examined, its recruitment understood, its organizations disrupted, and its claims challenged.

A useful explanation would have distinguished ordinary Muslim religious practice from Islamist political movements and violent jihadist organizations. Those categories involve different beliefs, conduct, and objectives. The declaration that Islam is a religion of peace offered Americans little help in understanding those distinctions.

YOUR ADMINISTRATION WAS ASKED TO EXPLAIN

This concern was raised while you were president. At an October 16, 2002, press briefing, a reporter challenged the administration’s characterization of Islam, citing passages of the Quran. Fleischer rejected the question’s premise and reaffirmed your position. He then argued against blaming innocent people or an entire religion for terrorists’ actions.

His defense of innocent people addressed collective blame. It did not resolve the underlying question about religious interpretation. Whether a particular passage supports the reporter’s reading requires examination of the text and its context. Reaffirming a presidential belief cannot perform that work.

That distinction remains significant. Defending a citizen against an unsupported accusation and evaluating a religious doctrine are different responsibilities. Your administration repeatedly answered questions about the second by emphasizing the first.

TWENTY-FIVE YEARS LATER, THE THREAT REMAINS

The Institute for Economics & Peace’s Global Terrorism Index 2026 identifies Islamic State, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, and al-Shabaab as the four deadliest terrorist organizations in 2025. Militant Islamist organizations remain central to the international terrorist threat a quarter-century after September 11.

The institute describes Islamic State’s dispersed affiliate network, JNIM’s expansion in the Sahel, the Pakistani Taliban’s resurgence, and al-Shabaab’s persistence despite military pressure. These organizations exploit instability and adapt to changing conditions. Their survival requires an explanation that examines both their ideology and the circumstances enabling their operations.

Their continuing violence does not establish that peaceful interpretations of Islam are insincere or nonexistent. It does establish that a general assurance about peace is insufficient to explain the movements committing that violence.

How did your declaration help Americans understand the religious arguments these organizations use to recruit followers and justify coercion?

THE EVIDENCE REQUIRES HONESTY IN BOTH DIRECTIONS

There is also evidence of improvement. The 2026 index reports that worldwide terrorism deaths declined by 28 percent in 2025. That is significant. An honest assessment must acknowledge progress alongside the persistence of dangerous organizations.

The existence of Islamist terrorism cannot establish the guilt of an individual Muslim. An accusation against a person requires evidence about that person. Religious affiliation alone cannot supply it. Your insistence that innocent Americans should be protected remains defensible.

But the existence of peaceful Muslims does not answer every criticism of Islamic teachings, religious institutions, or movements seeking political power. Personal innocence and institutional scrutiny are separate questions. Neither cancels the other.

Americans should be able to examine religious arguments for violence, restrictions on freedom of conscience, and demands for religious supremacy. Such inquiries require accurate sourcing and careful distinctions. They should receive substantive answers.

Religious freedom includes the freedom to question religion.

WHAT AMERICANS NEEDED TO HEAR

Mr. President, you could have affirmed that Muslim Americans possessed the same rights as everyone else while acknowledging that the attackers belonged to a movement whose religious arguments required serious examination.

You could have explained that the government would assess organizations through evidence about their teachings, financing, affiliations, and conduct. Public professions of peace would be considered alongside what those organizations actually supported.

You could have emphasized that peaceful worship would be protected and that recruitment for violence, threats, and assistance to terrorist organizations would receive scrutiny regardless of the religious language used to justify them.

That approach would have supplied an understandable standard: protect individual rights, investigate specific wrongdoing, and examine the ideology used to excuse it.

The phrase “Islam is a religion of peace” could reassure listeners. By itself, it could not answer their most consequential questions.

THE QUESTIONS STILL BEFORE YOU

Were you describing how peaceful Muslims understood their faith? Were you making a diplomatic statement intended to preserve cooperation? Were you offering a theological judgment? Were you attempting all three?

Those purposes are different. Each requires its own explanation.

Your September 17 speech clearly expressed concern about intimidation. It did not establish that your broad religious conclusion adequately accounted for competing interpretations or the movements acting upon them. Americans can recognize the value of your immediate purpose while challenging the reach of your words.

The record presented here also does not establish that you knowingly lied. That accusation would require evidence of your knowledge and intent. The criticism supported here is more precise: your administration offered a categorical religious assurance that did not adequately explain the enemy’s beliefs and methods.

THE FINDINGS

Your defense of innocent Muslim Americans was justified. Your administration’s declaration that Islam is a religion of peace went beyond defending their rights and provided an insufficient explanation of the ideological threat confronting the country.

Twenty-five years later, lethal Islamist organizations continue to operate. Their persistence requires scrutiny of the doctrines, institutions, networks, and conditions sustaining them. The documented decline in worldwide terrorism deaths also deserves acknowledgment.

Americans deserved leaders capable of defending religious liberty while examining religious claims used to authorize violence. Those responsibilities could—and should—have been fulfilled together.

Mr. President, you offered a memorable assurance. Twenty-five years later, Americans still deserve the explanation.

Respectfully,

Kim Wojcinski

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

text:
𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐍𝐞𝐰𝐬 – 𝐍𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟑, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔

Shrinking liquidity and forced selling drove a broad crypto retreat, even as institutions and developers continued building for digital assets.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰

Crypto’s sharp sell-off reflected a tightening supply of buyers as macroeconomic concerns met persistent outflows and leveraged positions unwound. Bitcoin fell below $70,000, with reported intraday lows near $67,500–$67,600, while Ethereum slipped under $2,000 and major altcoins weakened. Verified closes put BTC at $68,314 and ETH at $1,932. The pressure was reinforced by a $14.2 billion contraction in stablecoin supply over 30 days–the steepest monthly decline since June 2022–and roughly $1.44 billion in U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF outflows over five sessions. Above-forecast annual producer inflation and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy added to risk aversion; a softer monthly producer-price reading briefly eased pressure, but did not reverse the broader trend. Liquidations, concentrated in leveraged long positions, then amplified the decline. Yet the picture was not simply one of capitulation: Glassnode saw larger wallets accumulating and buy orders clustered around $68,000–$72,500, while ETF flows and other spot-demand measures remained weak. Alongside the drawdown, court-authorized action against funds linked to the Binance hack showed that tracing and freezing stolen assets can advance without implying recovery or a market sale.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐧𝐚𝐩𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐭

• $BTC: $68,314, -4.3%
• ETH: $1,932, -4.2%
• BNB: $630.70, -3.9%
• XRP: $1.01, -2.8%
• SOL: $78.26, -4.1%
• Sentiment: The Fear and Greed Index fell to 20, indicating extreme fear.
• Flows and liquidity: U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.44 billion in outflows over five sessions; stablecoin supply fell by $14.2 billion in the 30 days through Nov. 9.
• Macro: U.S. producer prices rose 6.5% year over year in October, though the monthly increase was 0.3%; a softer-than-expected monthly reading briefly weakened the dollar.
𝐓𝐨𝐩 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬

𝟏. 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐚𝐥 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐞𝐢𝐳𝐞 𝐨𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 $𝟏.𝟐 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐁𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐜𝐤

The U.S. Department of Justice obtained court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency linked to the Binance hack, attributed by the FBI to North Korean group TraderTraitor. More than $2.7 billion in stolen assets has been frozen through government and private-sector cooperation, while investigators continue tracing funds across blockchain networks. Binance estimated the theft at $6.34 billion and says it has replenished affected customer assets. The court-approved amount is part of the broader frozen total, not an additional recovery, and the action does not mean the cryptocurrency has been returned or sold. In a separate operation, authorities disrupted cloud infrastructure linked to FaceStealer, a scheme alleged to have stolen more than $400 million over 18 months using fake video meetings and malware.

𝟐. 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐝𝐞𝐞𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐧

Bitcoin’s break below $70,000 triggered heavy liquidations across crypto, with reports putting 24-hour losses in leveraged positions at roughly $1.2 billion to $1.65 billion; the majority were long positions. In one account, Bitcoin and Ethereum positions alone accounted for about $919 million and $289 million, respectively. These totals vary with reporting windows, but point to the same mechanism: price declines forced out traders positioned for a rebound, adding selling pressure. The drawdown coincided with $14.2 billion less stablecoin supply over 30 days and substantial withdrawals from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, while thin order-book depth left prices more vulnerable to large moves. Higher inflation expectations, rising Treasury yields and a stronger dollar further weighed on risk appetite.

𝟑. 𝐅𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐜𝐫𝐲𝐩𝐭𝐨 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞𝐝

President Trump nominated Steven Levine and Kristin Johnson to the Securities and Exchange Commission, and Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The four nominees require Senate confirmation; the CFTC candidates contributed to the CLARITY Act, which remains stalled in the Senate. The appointments could shape how the agencies approach digital assets, but their effect depends on confirmation and on the rules Congress and regulators ultimately pursue. Timing is tight: Senate confirmation proceedings face a December 18 adjournment target, while a change in Senate control is expected in January. The nominations therefore offer a possible route to filling agency vacancies, not an immediate resolution of the division of authority between the SEC and CFTC.

𝟒. 𝐏𝐍𝐂 𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐨𝐭𝐬 𝐔𝐒𝐃𝐂 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬

PNC is piloting a service through which eligible corporate clients can receive USDC on Ethereum and have it automatically converted one-for-one into U.S. dollars for deposit into their PNC accounts. Coinbase provides the payment infrastructure, while PNC supplies banking and treasury services. The structure is intended to let businesses accept stablecoin payments without holding digital assets. Whether it proves useful will depend on practical details such as processing time, fees and how failed transfers are handled, which have not been fully disclosed. The pilot adds a bank-led route for stablecoin payments, but does not yet establish how widely businesses will use it or what cost and speed advantages they will see.

𝟓. 𝐄𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐮𝐦 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐰𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐮𝐩𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐬𝐭

Ethereum’s staking ratio reached a record 36.3%, with roughly 44.5 million ETH locked, even as ETH fell below $2,000 amid ETF withdrawals and broader market selling. More ETH was waiting to enter staking than to exit, but the number of active validators had fallen from its September peak. The divergence suggests that rising staked supply does not, by itself, establish stronger market demand or improving price momentum. Separately, developers postponed Hoodi testnet testing for the Glamsterdam upgrade while reviewing possible effects on existing applications and smart contracts; no revised mainnet activation date was announced. Staking continues to absorb ETH, but it has not prevented the current downturn, and the upgrade delay leaves its near-term schedule unsettled.

𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 & 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲

The nominations of four SEC and CFTC candidates arrive as the CLARITY Act remains stalled, leaving the agencies’ future roles in digital-asset oversight unsettled. Their confirmation could fill vacancies and broaden participation in regulatory decisions, but the Senate’s limited time before its December 18 target adjournment makes the process uncertain. Meanwhile, prediction markets face competing claims of jurisdiction: the Justice Department and CFTC sued Arkansas, arguing that federal law gives the CFTC exclusive authority over event contracts, while states continue to pursue platforms over alleged unlicensed gambling. Louisiana obtained a temporary restraining order against several operators, with a hearing on further relief scheduled for November 30. These disputes are not resolved by the nominations; together, they show that crypto policy is being shaped both through agency appointments and court fights over which rules apply.

𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 & 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤

The Binance-linked seizure and FaceStealer disruption show how authorities can combine blockchain analysis, infrastructure seizures and cooperation with private firms to trace crypto-related crime, but neither action guarantees that victims will recover funds. Separate incidents highlight risks at the points where users access and control assets: Trezor found malicious implants in three Safe 5 wallets sold through CryptoBilis that could capture recovery phrases, while Unocoin suspended services during an investigation into suspicious transfers from wallets linked to BitGo. Chainstack also reported that weak access controls and exposed credentials contributed to its October incident, advising customers to change passwords, rotate node credentials and revoke old ones. Holders should treat recovery phrases as compromised if a device may have exposed them, and independently verify any recovery provider or unexpected request for payment.

𝐀𝐥𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬 & 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐬

The day’s protocol developments point to a continued push for institutional use, privacy and interoperability, even as falling prices and uncertain demand make adoption harder to assess. Injective opened governance voting on its Veyra upgrade, targeted for activation on November 24 if approved; the proposal would expand support for tokenized assets, cross-chain transfers and institutional trading tools, but voting remained below quorum. Akash opened a one-way migration portal allowing AKT holders to move tokens from Cosmos to Solana at a 1:1 ratio; staked tokens require a 21-day unbonding period, and moving the computing marketplace itself requires a separate vote. In parallel, the Solana Foundation released a beta toolkit for confidential AI applications on devnet, with hardware verification and private processing still in development. These launches add capabilities, but sustained use–not announcements alone–will determine whether they translate into lasting network activity.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐖𝐚𝐭𝐜𝐡

• November 16–30: Zcash community voting on the revised treasury proposal. Any implementation would require a future NU7.1 upgrade; no activation date is set.
• November 16: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is scheduled to lead a forum on AI’s effects on inflation, productivity and employment.
• November 19: Deadline for traders to join an existing squad in Bybit’s WSOT 2026 competition.
• November 24: Injective’s Veyra upgrade is targeted for activation if governance approves the proposal and the required quorum is reached.
• November 26: Thailand’s public-comment period closes on proposed stablecoin anti-money-laundering rules.
• November 30: Hearing on further relief in Louisiana’s case against prediction-market platforms; Upbit and Bithumb also plan to end MANTRA trading support after that date.
• December 18: Senate target adjournment date, relevant to confirmation proceedings for the SEC and CFTC nominees.

text:
Brian Banks (high school / college football prospect)
In 2002, Banks (then 16–17, a highly recruited linebacker from Long Beach Poly with scholarship offers including to USC) was accused by classmate Wanetta Gibson of kidnapping and raping her on campus. He maintained the encounter was consensual (or that no intercourse occurred). Facing a potential long sentence, he pleaded no contest, served about 5 years and 2 months in prison, spent time on parole, and registered as a sex offender—destroying his athletic prospects.
In 2011 (roughly 9 years later), Gibson contacted him via Facebook. In a recorded meeting with Banks and a private investigator, she recanted, saying there had been no rape or kidnapping. With help from the California Innocence Project, his conviction was vacated in 2012; he was cleared of sex-offender status and later briefly played in the UFL and with the Atlanta Falcons.
Gibson’s family had received a large civil settlement from the school district; she was reluctant to repeat the recantation publicly for fear of having to repay it. A court later ordered her to repay related funds

text:
New York City's Council voted 44 to 5 on Thursday to ban companies from using your personal data to set your price.

In a Consumer Reports test of Instacart, 74% of the grocery items checked were shown to shoppers at more than one price.

While the measure is supported by Mamdani, no reports have come out about him signing the measure as of 14 Nov.

He has 30 days to sign the legislation, though if he doesn't, the bill will become law anyway, and it will come into effect one year from then.

The legislation prohibits businesses from using personal information and algorithms to set different prices on the same product for different individuals.

Companies can be fined up to $1,000 per violation, and each customer or transaction can be counted separately. The bill will allow loyalty programs and real price reductions.

The Consumer Reports trial didn't find any evidence that prices tracked ZIP code or income levels, and Instacart called its tests randomized and ended them in December 2025. Delta told senators it has never used a fare that targets individuals based on personal data.

Uber has pushed back on the bill, while Speaker Menin said it is flatly incorrect that businesses cannot offer reductions.

In an Instacart trial in a Safeway grocery store in Washington, DC, the same box of corn flakes was quoted as $2.99, $3.49 and $3.69. That's a difference of up to 23%.

Consumer Reports estimated variation like that could cost a family of four $1,200 a year. Would you back this ban on personalized prices?
